title: I Was Wrong About ChatGPT and AI (Part 2 of 3): What I'm Not Saying and Why I'm Interested hy-im-interested
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: In Part 2 of his three-part AI series, Stuart clarifies what his ChatGPT reversal does not mean — he is not endorsing "tech-ification of learning" or teacher replacement — and explains why the technology has nonetheless captured his attention. He commits to three things regardless of AI's advance: his classroom will keep relying primarily on analog spiral notebooks, his goal remains developing better thinkers and readers rather than device-dependent students, and students will still need to know and argue about a lot of content, since thinking well with AI output requires prior knowledge, not less of it. He then compares the current AI moment to his early blogging years covering the Common Core, arguing AI is fundamentally different because it isn't a single static document, isn't single-sourced, isn't confined to education, and isn't confined to the United States — citing GPT's parameter-count growth as evidence of its "hockey stick" trajectory. The piece sets up Part 3, where he promises to address what he thinks AI will and won't ultimately change about teaching.
points: Stuart draws a hard line between being "interested" in AI and being "sold" on it, explicitly rejecting the idea that his AI curiosity signals a pedagogical shift toward tech-centered instruction.

His tool analogy — give me a chainsaw and I chop a log, give an ice sculptor a chainsaw and she makes a miracle — restates his "user X tool = output" thesis: AI is a multiplier of existing skill, not a replacement for it.
He explicitly argues that AI makes prior knowledge more important, not less, since thinking well "with" AI-generated content requires the same base of things known and argued as thinking without it.

The Common-Core comparison is his central rhetorical device for explaining why AI deserves sustained attention rather than the same wait-it-out skepticism he applied to past edu-fads: unlike a static PDF standard, AI's capability is on an exponential growth curve.
quotes: I'm not writing this AI series because I'm sold on the tech-ification of learning or replacing teachers with AIs. It's the opposite of those two things, actually.

No matter how useful AIs like ChatGPT become, my classes will still primarily rely on the technology of 70-cent spiral notebooks. We'll take notes, we'll write short answer responses, we'll free-write, we'll reflect — by hand.

Right now, AI is like that — it's a multiplier of the user's ability to think well with the tool. And so, the only way to help my students think well that I'm aware of is the same as it's always been.

I've long accepted what cognitive scientists have: getting a computer to produce knowledge is a Grand Canyon's chasm away from being able to think well with that knowledge. You've got to know things — lots of things — in order to comprehend what you read or hear, to argue well, to think clearly or deeply.
In eleven years, the document hasn't changed. The world has, but the document hasn't. It's stuck in time, like the mosquito in Jurassic Park.
AIs like ChatGPT are the total opposite of this. Their rate of change is literally exponential.
In short, AI has my attention because whether you're looking at parameter count or training data set sizes or companies involved or users of the technology, you're looking at hockey stick growth.
